title: The First Minutes
description: Danger, response, airway and breathing, the recovery position, and when CPR applies
tryIt: With a willing friend lying on a soft floor, practise rolling them into the recovery position using St John Ambulance's steps, then swap places.

concepts.title: How it works: why the order matters
concepts.contentHtml:
A shout from up the trail. Your friend has slipped on wet rock and is lying very still at the bottom of a gully, and every instinct says run. First aid says something different: look before you leap, because a second casualty helps nobody. After that, the order in which you check things is not arbitrary. It follows whatever kills fastest.

The airway comes early because of a simple piece of anatomy. As the British Red Cross explains, when a person is unresponsive, their muscles relax and their tongue can block their airway so they can no longer breathe.1 Tilting the head back opens the airway by pulling the tongue forward. If the heart has stopped, the clock runs faster still: Resuscitation Council UK warns that for every minute someone is in cardiac arrest without CPR and a defibrillator, their chance of survival falls by 10%.2

Organised first aid is younger than you might think. A Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, arrived near the northern Italian town of Solferino in time to witness one of the bloodiest battles of the nineteenth century,3 and stayed to help the wounded. In 1862 he published a small book, A Memory of Solferino, calling for better care for wounded soldiers, and the committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross first met in Geneva in February 1863.4 In England, the St John Ambulance Association was established in 1877 to provide training in first aid.5

Chest compressions arrived later still, and partly by accident. William Kouwenhoven, who held a doctorate in electrical engineering, rediscovered external cardiac compression during his research on defibrillation6 at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. In 1960 he reported a 70% survival rate in twenty patients,7 and argued that anyone, anywhere could start resuscitation: ‘All that is needed are two hands.’

concepts.title: In the field: danger, response, airway, breathing
concepts.contentHtml:
St John Ambulance calls its checklist the primary survey; Resuscitation Council UK boils the opening down to three steps: check, call, CPR.1 In order:

  1. Danger. Before you go near, make sure the area is safe.
  2. Response. Kneel by their chest, gently shake their shoulders2 and ask loudly, ‘Are you OK?’
  3. Shout and call. No response? Shout for help and get someone to call 999 or 112, or put your own phone on speaker and call.
  4. Pouring blood first. If blood is gushing or spurting, press on the wound before you deal with the airway.3
  5. Airway. One hand on the forehead to tilt the head back, two fingers to lift the chin.
  6. Breathing. Look, listen and feel for 10 seconds.
  7. Breathing normally? Recovery position, and keep checking. Not breathing normally? Start CPR: push down hard in the centre of the chest and release, twice per second, without stopping,4 while the ambulance call handler helps you. Send a helper for a defibrillator, but if you are alone, do not leave the casualty to look for one.5

For the recovery position, St John Ambulance's method is to kneel beside them, place the nearest arm at a right angle with the palm up, bring the far arm across so the back of their hand rests against their cheek, pull the far knee up, then roll them towards you and tilt the head back. After 30 minutes, roll them onto the other side.6

Safety Call emergency services first whenever you can: 999 or 112 in the UK, 911 in the US. If you are remote and cannot call, St John Ambulance's advice is to send two people for help together.7 And be honest with yourself: a page cannot train your hands. St John Ambulance and the British Red Cross run hands-on first aid courses, and nothing here replaces one.

concepts.title: Myth check: gasps, ribs and lawsuits
concepts.contentHtml:
Two beliefs stop people helping at exactly the moment help matters most.

Myth If they are gasping, they are breathing, so CPR is not needed.
Reality In the first minutes of cardiac arrest, St John Ambulance says, about half of casualties do something called agonal gasping:1 slow, sometimes noisy gasps, with the mouth opening and the neck stretching. It is not normal breathing. It is a sign of cardiac arrest, and the British Red Cross is clear that noisy, irregular or gasping breathing means start chest compressions.2
Myth CPR could break their ribs or land you in court, so it is safer not to try.
Reality You might crack a rib, the British Red Cross admits, but a damaged rib will mend, and without compressions their chances of survival are much lower.3 Press on someone who turns out to be breathing and there is no evidence you will cause serious damage.4 As for the law, Resuscitation Council UK says it is very unlikely that anyone in the UK acting in good faith would be held liable, and no such action has ever been brought against someone who performed CPR.5

Wait, really? You do not need training to use a defibrillator. St John Ambulance says AEDs are built so that anyone, even without any training, can use them in an emergency.6 Switch one on and it talks you through every step: it checks the heart's rhythm and only sends a shock if one is needed. For an adult, one pad goes on the upper right side of the chest just beneath the collarbone and the other on the lower left side, below the armpit.7

title: Stop the Bleeding
description: Direct pressure, packing a deep wound, and what current guidance says about tourniquets
tryIt: Press a clean folded tea towel firmly onto a friend's forearm as if it were a wound, then bandage over it and try St John Ambulance's five-second nail-press test for circulation.

concepts.title: How it works: plugging the leak
concepts.contentHtml:
The knife skids off a knot in your kindling and opens your forearm. There is blood, a lot of it, and for a second you just stare. Use that second. Bleeding is a plumbing problem, and the first answer is the simplest one in this course.

Pressure works because you become the plug. The British Red Cross puts it plainly: you are acting as a plug to stop the blood escaping,1 and the pressure you apply helps the blood clot. Lose too much and you slide towards shock, which St John Ambulance describes as the body not having enough blood circulating to supply the vital organs with oxygen.2

Most bleeding stops with pressure. A life-threatening bleed does not. St John Ambulance calls it extreme bleeding likely to cause death in minutes,3 and gives three signs: blood pumping from the wound, bleeding that pressure cannot stop or slow, and blood quickly soaking through bandage after bandage.4

The tourniquet, a strap that squeezes a limb shut, is ancient. Its first documented use was not for bleeding at all: Hindu physicians in the 6th century BCE used one to treat Greek troops bitten by snakes5 they did not recognise. The first reported use to control bleeding from a wound came from a French army surgeon, Etienne Morel, in 1674,6 and the word comes from the French tourner, ‘to turn’.

concepts.title: In the field: pressure, packing and tourniquets
concepts.contentHtml:
St John Ambulance sums up severe bleeding in seven words: your priority is to stop the bleeding.1

  1. Gloves if you have them. Then expose the wound, cutting clothing away if you must.
  2. Press hard, right on it, with a sterile dressing or a clean, non-fluffy cloth. The casualty can press too.
  3. Something stuck in it? Leave it in: it may be plugging the hole. Press on either side instead.
  4. Call 999 or 112, on speaker if you are alone, and say where the wound is and how bad it is.
  5. Bandage firmly over the pad, then test it: press a nail beyond the bandage for five seconds. If the colour has not come back within two seconds, the bandage is too tight.2
  6. If pressure fails. On the head, neck, chest or abdomen, a haemostatic dressing is held tightly for at least five minutes and sometimes packed tightly into the wound.3 On a limb, a tourniquet goes close to and above the injury, never on a joint,4 tightened until the bleeding stops, with the time noted.
  7. Watch for shock. Help them lie down on a rug or blanket and keep them warm.

No tourniquet? Ambulance control may talk you through an improvised one: St John Ambulance lists a triangular bandage, scarf or tie with a pen or fork as the rod, or a belt pulled tight.5

Safety Call 999 or 112 first. A tourniquet hurts, so warn the casualty, and once it is on, never loosen it. Do not wash a heavily bleeding wound,6 which the British Red Cross says may make it bleed more. Public bleed control kits, often kept beside defibrillators, are meant for anyone to use7 and come with instructions. None of this replaces a hands-on course.

concepts.title: Myth check: the tourniquet's bad name
concepts.contentHtml:
Few pieces of kit have been as feared as the tourniquet, or as misunderstood.

Myth A tourniquet means losing the limb.
Reality The fear has a history. On old battlefields evacuation could take days, surgery was rudimentary and there were no antibiotics, so limbs were often lost, and the amputations were then blamed on tourniquets.1 Modern figures look very different. In one series of 110 tourniquets applied before hospital, 5.5% caused nerve complications and none resulted in limb loss,2 and after the Boston Marathon bombings 27 tourniquets were applied with no adverse outcomes reported.3 Most bleeding still stops with direct pressure; the tourniquet is for when it does not.
Myth Loosen it every so often to let some blood back into the limb.
Reality This was once official advice. The US Army's 1992 survival manual, FM 21-76, said a buddy could release the pressure every 10 to 15 minutes for 1 or 2 minutes.4 Current St John Ambulance guidance is blunt: once a tourniquet is applied it should not be loosened, because the bleeding will start again.5 Note the time and leave it for the hospital.

Wait, really? During the First World War, a British medical manual, Injuries and Diseases of War, spectacularly criticised tourniquets.6 Yet in 2006 the US Army Institute of Surgical Research reported higher survival when tourniquets went on before hospital than when they were applied in hospital: 89% against 78%.7

title: Heat and Cold
description: How the body loses heat, hypothermia and frostbite, heat exhaustion and heatstroke
tryIt: On your next cold walk, pack a hat, a dry spare layer and a sit mat, and at a rest stop compare how fast you chill sitting on bare ground and on the mat.

concepts.title: How it works: the 37-degree engine
concepts.contentHtml:
Sleet is coming sideways off the ridge. An hour ago your friend was moaning about the cold; now they have gone quiet, they keep fumbling the zip of their jacket and their words are slurring. The quiet is the frightening part.

Your core runs at about 37°C, held within half a degree.1 When you cool, the blood vessels in your skin narrow to keep warm blood in the core, and shivering can raise your heat production to as much as five times normal.2 Heat leaks out four ways:3 conduction into cold ground, convection as wind strips warm air away, evaporation from wet skin and clothes, and radiation straight off the skin.

Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C,4 and it does not need a blizzard: the CDC notes it can happen even above 40°F (about 4°C) if someone is chilled by rain, sweat or cold water.5 Worse, low body temperature affects the brain, so a person may not know it is happening and won't be able to do anything about it.6 Clinicians stage it by signs:7 mild (35–32°C), conscious and shivering; moderate (below 32 to 28°C), with impaired consciousness and shivering that may stop; severe (below 28°C), unconscious.

None of this is new: hypothermia has been recognised since ancient times,8 a disease of war and of disasters such as avalanches and earthquakes.9 Heat kills too. In heatstroke the body can no longer control its temperature: the sweating mechanism fails, and the CDC warns that body temperature can rise to 106°F (41°C) or higher within 10 to 15 minutes.10

concepts.title: In the field: warming up and cooling down
concepts.contentHtml:
Cold and heat need opposite fixes but the same first move: call for help, then change the casualty's surroundings.

  1. Out of the wind. Indoors if you can; if not, the most sheltered spot nearby, with your body as a windbreak.
  2. Wet off, dry on. Replace wet clothing and cover their head, but do not give them your own clothes: you need to stay warm too.1
  3. Off the ground. Lay them on a thick layer of dry insulation such as pine branches, heather or bracken,2 inside a sleeping bag, blankets or a foil blanket.
  4. Call 999 or 112, and stay. Never leave them alone.
  5. Fuel. If they are fully alert, warm drinks and high-energy food such as chocolate.3
  6. Frostbite. Indoors, remove rings, gloves and boots and warm the part gently in your lap with your hands, then in warm (not hot) water at around 40°C.4 Dry it, add a light dressing and raise it. Do not thaw it if it could freeze again.5
  7. Too hot. Move them somewhere cool, strip extra layers, give plenty of water, and spray or sponge them with cool water while fanning. They should feel better within 30 minutes.6 If not, or if they are confused, call 999: treat it as heatstroke and keep cooling with a cool, wet sheet, sponging and fanning.
Safety Handle a very cold person gently and keep them lying flat if they cannot walk:7 a medical review of hypothermia notes that collapse during rescue is most often triggered by sudden movement.8 No hot baths, hot water bottles or heat lamps.9 If someone with heatstroke becomes unresponsive, use the recovery position and be ready to give CPR.

concepts.title: Myth check: snow, brandy and sweat
concepts.contentHtml:
Cold and heat both breed folklore, and some of it does real harm.

Myth Rub frostbitten skin, or rub it with snow, to get the blood going.
Reality The NHS, St John Ambulance and the CDC all say do not rub or massage it, and St John Ambulance warns that rubbing could damage the skin.1 Keep it away from fires, radiators and stoves too: frozen skin may be numb, so victims of frostbite can harm themselves further.2
Myth A nip of brandy warms you up.
Reality St John Ambulance says alcohol will make hypothermia worse,3 and the NHS lists it firmly under things not to do. The CDC counts people who drink alcohol in excess among those at high risk of hypothermia4 in the first place.
Myth If they are still sweating, it cannot be heatstroke.
Reality The NHS lists hot skin without sweating among the signs,5 but the CDC's list for heat stroke reads hot, dry skin or profuse sweating.6 Do not wait for the skin to dry. Confusion, slurred speech, a fit or collapse in the heat means call 999 and start cooling.

Wait, really? Warming someone up does not instantly stop them cooling. In hypothermia, a medical review notes, the heart can even stop from afterdrop: further cooling, even after rewarming has started,7 mainly because blood starts flowing again through cold parts of the body.8

title: Burns, Sprains and Breaks
description: Twenty minutes of cool water, looking after a sprain, and improvised slings and splints
tryIt: Tie an arm sling on a willing friend with a triangular bandage or a large scarf, following St John Ambulance's steps, and check it supports the arm to the tip of the little finger.

concepts.title: How it works: heat in skin, force in bone
concepts.contentHtml:
The billy can tips. Boiling water sheets across the back of your hand, and as you leap away your foot goes down a rabbit hole. Two injuries in two seconds, and both have the same enemy: time.

With a burn, time is damage. St John Ambulance puts it simply: the longer the burning goes on, the more severe the injury.1 That is why cooling is treatment, not comfort. The British Red Cross says it reduces pain, swelling and the risk of scarring,2 and the sooner and longer a burn is cooled with running water, the less the impact.3 Burns are a global killer too: the WHO estimates that around 163 000 people died in 2023 from fire, heat and hot substances.4

Bones and joints fail in different ways. A sprain is a torn or twisted ligament, the tissue that connects the joints;5 a strain is an overstretched or torn muscle. A fracture is a broken bone, and the British Red Cross notes that whether it is cracked, snapped, crushed or in pieces, the first aid is the same.6 In an open fracture there is a wound in the skin near the break; in a closed one the skin is intact.

Keeping a broken bone still once decided who lived. The Thomas splint, invented in 1865 by the Welsh orthopaedic surgeon Hugh Owen Thomas,7 held a broken leg steady. In the First World War, thigh fractures were common and early survival was poor. Thomas's nephew Robert Jones, made Consultant Orthopaedic Surgeon to the British Army in December 1914,8 championed the splint, and once it was routinely supplied from 1917 it dramatically reduced death rates.9

concepts.title: In the field: cool, cover, support
concepts.contentHtml:
Burns first, because the clock is running.

  1. Cool it. Hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible and within 3 hours.1 No tap? Use cool bottled water, a wet towel, or even cold milk or canned drinks.2
  2. Off with rings and watches and nearby clothing before it swells, but leave anything stuck to the burn.
  3. Cover it loosely with cling film laid along it, not wrapped round,3 or a clean plastic bag over a hand or foot.
  4. Call 999 for a burn that is large or deep, on the face, genitals or bottom, or caused by chemicals or electricity.
  5. Sprain? For the first 2 to 3 days the NHS suggests PRICE: protection, rest, ice wrapped in a tea towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, compression and elevation.4
  6. Suspected break? Ask them to keep still and support the limb by holding the joint above and below the injury,5 with padding such as clothing or a blanket around it. Unless they are in danger, do not move them until it is secured: an arm in a sling, a leg with broad-fold bandages.6
  7. Open fracture? Cover the wound with a clean dressing and press around it, never on the bone.

To make an arm sling, St John Ambulance's steps are: support the arm, slide a triangular bandage under it with the point at the elbow, take the top end round the back of the neck, fold the lower end up over the forearm to the shoulder, and tie a reef knot above the collarbone.7

Safety Call 999 or 112 for open fractures, broken long bones and any suspected back, neck or pelvis injury. Never force a limb straight or push a joint back into place.8 Cool the burn, not the person: a whole body in a cold bath or shower can bring on hypothermia.9 Do not burst blisters.

concepts.title: Myth check: butter, ice and wiggling toes
concepts.contentHtml:
Kitchen wisdom gets burns badly wrong, and playground wisdom does the same for broken bones.

Myth Butter, or toothpaste, soothes a burn.
Reality They do the opposite. The British Red Cross points out that butter and cream contain oils, and oils retain heat,1 while the menthol in toothpaste only gives a superficial feeling of cooling.2 The NHS says no creams, oils or butter, and the WHO adds toothpaste and traditional pastes.3 Anything you smear on may have to be removed in hospital, causing more pain.4
Myth Ice is the quickest way to cool a burn.
Reality St John Ambulance says do not use ice, creams or gels, which may cause damage and increase the risk of infection.5 Cool running water is the treatment.
Myth If you can move it or stand on it, it isn't broken.
Reality Not necessarily, says the British Red Cross: the only accurate way to diagnose a broken bone is an X-ray,6 and it is usually impossible to tell a break from a sprain without one.7 If in doubt, get medical advice.

Wait, really? If there is no running water, the British Red Cross suggests pouring other cold liquids over the burn, such as milk, soft drinks or even beer.8 What matters is the cold, not the drink.

title: Bites, Stings and Infection
description: Snakes, stings and ticks, keeping a wound clean, and the myths that make things worse
tryIt: Pack a small wound kit with gloves, sterile dressings, plasters, fine-tipped tweezers and a bottle of clean water, and practise the NHS cleaning steps on a pretend graze drawn in pen.

concepts.title: How it works: venom and germs
concepts.contentHtml:
You reach for a log on a sunny heath and feel a sharp jab on the back of your hand. Two small punctures. Something grey-brown slides away into the heather. Breathe: in Britain, the odds are firmly on your side.

The NHS says most snake bites in the UK are not serious.1 Only three snakes live wild in Britain and the adder is the only venomous one: grey or reddish-brown, with a dark zig-zag stripe down its back.2 Worldwide the picture is grimmer. The WHO estimates that 5.4 million people are bitten by snakes each year3 and that 81 410 to 137 880 die,4 many of them farmers and children in poor rural communities. Venom can cause paralysis that may prevent breathing, bleeding disorders and tissue damage, and antivenom, given in hospital, is the most effective treatment.5

Germs are the slower threat. In 1867 the surgeon Joseph Lister described a new practice: since Louis Pasteur had shown that putrefaction was caused by minute organisms in the air,6 Lister dressed wounds with carbolic acid to kill them, starting with compound fractures,7 where decay did the most harm. One danger of a muddy wound today is tetanus, which the NHS says can follow soil or manure getting into a wound such as a bite, burn or scratch;8 in the UK the vaccine has been routinely given since 1961.9

Small creatures bring their own risks: the NHS notes that ticks can spread Lyme disease,10 and for a few people a single bee sting can trigger anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that St John Ambulance says can develop just seconds after contact.11

concepts.title: In the field: bites, stings and clean wounds
concepts.contentHtml:
Different creatures, one rule: call for help early for any snakebite, any sting in the mouth or throat, and anyone struggling to breathe.

  1. Snakebite. Call 999 or 112. Keep the bitten part as still as you can,1 stay calm, take off rings and loosen clothing in case it swells, and note the snake's colour and pattern (a photo from a safe distance helps). The CDC adds: do not drive yourself, and mark the edge of the swelling on the skin with the time.2
  2. Bee or wasp sting. Scrape the stinger out sideways with a fingernail or the edge of a bank card. Not tweezers: they can squeeze out more poison.3 Wash with soap and water, then hold something cold on it.
  3. Anaphylaxis (swollen lips or tongue, wheezing, collapse): help them use their adrenaline auto-injector, or use it yourself,4 and call 999.
  4. Jellyfish. Rinse with seawater, not fresh water,5 lift out any spines with tweezers or a card edge, then soak in water as hot as they can bear for at least 30 minutes.6
  5. Tick. Grip it close to the skin with fine-tipped tweezers and pull away with steady, even pressure.7 Do not twist or jerk it. Then wash.
  6. Small cut or graze. Wash your hands, rinse the wound with tap or bottled water,8 pat it dry, clean the skin around it with soap and water wiping away from the wound, and cover it.
Safety Get medical help if a wound still has soil or dirt in it after cleaning, if you are not fully vaccinated against tetanus, or if it becomes red, swollen, more painful or oozes pus.9 Outside the UK, call the local emergency number for any snakebite.

concepts.title: Myth check: cut, suck and pee
concepts.contentHtml:
Bites and stings attract more folk remedies than almost anything else in first aid. Three of the most stubborn:

Myth Cut the bite and suck out the venom, then tie it off.
Reality This once had official backing. The US Army's 1992 survival manual told soldiers that if help was more than an hour away they could make small cuts over the fang marks and use suction, and to put a constricting band between the bite and the heart. Today's guidance is clear. The NHS says do not suck or cut the venom out of the bite and do not tie anything tightly round it;1 the CDC adds no tourniquet, no ice and no slashing the wound in any way.2
Myth Pee on a jellyfish sting.
Reality The NHS list of things not to do starts with exactly this: do not pee on the sting.3 It also rules out ice or a cold pack.4 Rinse with seawater and use heat instead.
Myth Burn a tick off with a match, or smother it in petroleum jelly or nail polish so it lets go.
Reality The CDC warns against petroleum jelly, heat and nail polish: they may agitate the tick and force infected fluid from it into the skin.5 Tweezers and a steady pull win.

Wait, really? The tourniquet's first documented use, in the 6th century BCE, was for snakebite.6 Two and a half thousand years later, snakebite is exactly where the NHS and the CDC say not to use one.
